# **Precious metal forecast** 

_Gold, silver, platinum and palladium prices in 2012_ 

**David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** 

**05 January 2012** 

#### **New York:** 

- We remain bullish for precious metal prices throughout 2012 as a whole, although we expect depressing developed world economic conditions and Euro weakness to present considerable challenges to attaining higher prices earlier in the year. Gold and palladium are expected to outperform platinum and gold.

## **<mark>Overview</mark>** 

At the start of 2011, we were bullish in our outlook for precious metals prices. However, we noted that slowing developed world economic activity and European debt concerns could prove problematic. The sell-off at the end of the year was therefore not entirely unexpected but it was deeper than we had previously thought likely, with prices weakening more than expected, and only the gold price recording an annual gain despite periods of strength for the other metals. 

Looking into 2012, we are once again positive in our outlook for precious metals prices, albeit from lower levels for palladium, platinum and silver. However, of the four main precious metals, we only foresee gold and palladium averaging more during 2012 than they did last year. 

Many of the global concerns which dominated the news in 2011 will be important this year too. Interest rates in the developed world are very unlikely to rise. Economic growth is set to be weak, although the USA looks somewhat healthier than had been expected a few months ago. Quantitative easing looks less likely in America than before now that the economy there is showing some positive signs of health. European debt concerns will be a major influence on the markets whatever happens, although we expect the Euro to continue as a viable currency. Some form of European quantitative easing seems increasingly likely, suggesting that there could be further boosts to a range of asset prices. 

By contrast, in the developing world, inflation is high and growth rates are rather better than in the more developed economies. There will therefore be higher physical demand for many commodities from consumers, al

though expectations of strengthening demand may already be built into prices to some extent. 

Amongst the precious metals, end user demand seems most robust for palladium with demand for silver and platinum being less positive. Precious metal demand in China should be healthy but Indian purchasing will weaken unless the Rupee firms against the Dollar. North American demand for the more industrial metals should be decent but a European recession will weigh on purchases of the three white metals there. Investor interest is likely to be more positive for gold as a “safe”-ish haven and for platinum and palladium, based on their positive longer term market fundamentals. 

Along with the impact of insipid developed world demand for some of these metals, we expect the Euro to weaken against the Dollar as European governments struggle to solve the region’s debt, unemployment and growth problems, leading to a challenging period in early 2012 for precious metals prices. However, prospects look better for higher metal prices later in the year as the risk of holding the Euro gradually decreases. 

## **<mark>Competition from other assets</mark>** 

For an investor, the precious metal complex does not exist in a vacuum. To attract investment, and increase in value, these metals must either appear to have better prospects of price appreciation, or exhibit the benefits of diversification of assets or of being a safe haven, or show some other attribute which makes them more attractive than other assets to investors. 

Currently, bond yields for a few favoured countries are extremely low as quantitative easing has increased bond prices and investors have fled to those currencies perceived as safest. Although long term bond yields appear to be unattractive in general, the perception of these few favoured countries’ bonds (American, British, German and Japanese in particular) as safe, even if they are not risk-free, means that they will remain favoured while the risk of European defaults remains. We are unlikely to see large flows of capital out of the bond market into commodities during this period of high perceived risk. However, with yields already extraordinarily low, only a sharp worsening of economic sentiment can be expected to drive further investment into bonds.

In the equities markets, valuations are now low enough to make some shares attractive on a yield basis alone. The prospect of reasonable global economic growth suggests that some capital appreciation might be expected too, particularly where the relevant equity benefits from high developing world growth rates. However, risk aversion and price volatility are likely to make equity investment only for the brave in early 2012 unless equity prices make a determined move higher or price volatility decreases. 

Within the commodity sector, last year’s surprisingly weak performance may deter some investors fr

om further speculative activity. However, the negatives associated with other asset markets mean that we still expect to see plenty of active investors in the commodities. Here, the investment argument is principally between cyclical and noncyclical commodities. Although the global economy is likely to grow, in the absence of a Euro break-up, growth is set to slow. Less cyclical commodities are likely to be favoured, while fear of a further global slowdown persists, with gold a potential beneficiary. The other precious metals are more exposed to industrial demand and could underperform gold in this scenario, more in line with agricultural commodities or some base metals. 

## **<mark>Gold</mark>** 

2012 Forecast High: $2,075, Average: $1,770, Low: $1,480 

Sentiment on gold has recently turned significantly less bullish or, in some cases, actually bearish. In part this is due to the challenges of believing that gold can extend its decade long run of annual gains and, in part, to the fall in prices during late 2011. 

However, many of the underlying driving forces for higher gold prices in 2011 will persist this year. Extreme economic uncertainty, low real interest rates, high developing world inflation and the prospect of European sovereign debt defaults will accompany us throughout 2012. We are, though, concerned that risk fatigue seems to be developing with ever greater market stresses needed to drive fresh gold buying interest. Signs of price sensitivity in the Indian physical market are also negative. 

Nonetheless, with the Eurozone’s problems unlikely to be solved quickly and the sustainability of the US debt position and deficit likely to come back into focus at some point, the desire to diversify from cash into gold should remain strong, whether for the official sector, rich Chinese and Indian investors or concerned Europeans. Overall, we see good reasons to own gold. The motivation to buy more gold may be more limited than before, but we do not see good reasons to dispose of any gold investments, even following the decline in price in H2 2011. 

We do not expect the Euro to fracture but some Euro weakness can be expected early in the year, limiting how far gold can move in USD terms in H1. However, we expect a stronger H2 for the Euro against the US Dollar and we, along with most of the market, would be surprised if gold does not challenge last year’s nominal highs during 2012. 

## **<mark>Silver</mark>** 

### 2012 Forecast High: $44.60, Average: $30.95, Low: $19.20 

Silver demand weakened during the second half of 2011, reflecting cuts in government subsidies and the reduction of stocks in the photovoltaic sector, slowing sales of plasma televisions and lethargic purchasing from some other industries. This weakness was confirmed by an increase in COMEX inventories during the same period. We expect the first half of 2012 to be similar in demand terms with upwards pressure on the US Dollar contributing to some price weakness. Supplies

of silver should rise in 2012, increasing the

scale of the likely surplus in the first half of the year. If the silver price does move higher, then further producer hedging should contribute additional supplies. 

If the global economy continues to grow as we expect, the market could tighten in the second half of the year and prices should firm. Overall, though, investors will be key: physical investment demand should remain robust; ETF flows are likely to be less supportive than in 2010 but may be more positive than in 2011. Investor interest on COMEX is low by historical standards and there is certainly room for a concerted push higher in price at some point this year. A high gold price should be supportive of silver throughout, too, and we are slightly bullish for this metal over the next twelve months overall. 

## **<mark>Platinum</mark>** 

2012 Forecast High: $1,875, Average: $1,575, Low: $1,305 

The fourth quarter of 2011 provided a lesson for those who believe the platinum price is driven by fundamentals. The gold-platinum spread has started to act as a barometer of market risk and the extended troubles of the Eurozone suggest that gold will trade at a premium to platinum for the first part of 2012 at least. Nonetheless, with a rising gold price expected later in the year, we can be fairly positive about the outlook for the platinum price towards the end of 2012. 

In fundamental terms, although a high cost of production could support the price in the long term, we expect few significant cuts in mine production of platinum during 2012 to drive the price higher in the shorter term. End user demand will be needed to help investors drive any price rises and a weak outlook for European automotive output (and hence platinum use) is worrying. We expect the global economic outlook to improve, aiding industrial platinum demand, and jewellery demand seems to be robust in China, suggesting that some move towards higher prices is likely later in the year. However, with relatively weak fundamentals, it seems unlikely that platinum will trade at an average price in excess of last year’s level. 

## **<mark>Palladium</mark>** 

2012 Forecast High: $860, Average: $745, Low: $565 

The palladium price confounded expectations in 2011 by falling in the second half of the year as investors sold their positions as the economic outlook worsened. In simple terms, speculators are now less exposed to this metal but remain firm believers in the underlying bullish fundamentals of strong automotive demand, limited scope for additional mine production, and the fact that Russian state stocks of this metal must, eventually, run out. 

We feel that these are all reasonable indicators of strong future palladium prices but it is not clear that most of the potential gains will be made during 2012. The outlook for the global automotive industry is positive (although much fo

rward buying has already taken place) and economic growth should drive enhanced palladium demand from the electronics sector. There is little or no demand side price elasticity at current levels, so this market should move into a “fundamental” deficit if the Eurozone crisis does not worsen. 

ETF selling which presented a headwind for prices in 2011 should slow and we therefore expect higher prices, with a reasonable possibility that palladium should outperform platinum in percentage terms during 2012. However, we feel that prices in excess of $800 an ounce may prove attractive for profit-taking by investors, imposing some form of price ceiling.
